topic: Countries moving to ban social media for children
headline_marked: [[Over 10 countries are moving to ban social media]] for children under 16, led by Australia
headline: Over 10 countries are moving to ban social media for children under 16, led by Australia
summary: Australia was the first to implement a social media ban for children under 16, with penalties up to $34.4 million USD for non-compliant companies. Many other nations are now drafting similar legislation to protect young users.
details: A growing number of countries are proposing or implementing bans on social media for children and teens, aiming to mitigate risks like cyberbullying, addiction, and mental health issues. Australia led the way, becoming the first to ban social media for children under 16, effective December 2025.

Australia's ban covers platforms like Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and X, requiring companies to implement robust age verification methods beyond self-declaration. Non-compliance could result in fines up to $49.5 million AUD ($34.4 million USD).

Critics, including Amnesty Tech, raise concerns about privacy, excessive government intervention, and the effectiveness of such bans, arguing they might ignore the realities of younger generations. Despite these concerns, several nations are advancing with their legislative plans.

Austria plans to ban social media for under-14s, with draft legislation expected by June. Canada introduced a digital safety bill for under-16s, allowing companies to bypass the ban with strong protective policies.

Denmark aims to ban social media for children under 15, with plans to become law by mid-2026, supported by a new 'digital evidence' app for age verification. France passed a bill to ban under-15s, awaiting Senate approval.

Germany's conservatives proposed a ban for under-16s, though coalition partners showed hesitation. Greece will ban under-15s from January 2027, citing rising anxiety and sleep problems among children.
Indonesia is banning under-16s from platforms like YouTube, TikTok, and Facebook. Malaysia also plans to implement a ban for under-16s this year, announced in November 2025.

Poland is drafting legislation to prohibit under-15s from social media. Slovenia is also working on similar legislation for under-15s, focusing on content-sharing networks like TikTok and Instagram. Spain's prime minister announced plans for an under-16 ban, pending parliamentary approval.

topic: US solar energy surpasses coal for first time
headline_marked: [[Solar power generated more electricity than coal]] in the US for the first time in May
headline: Solar power generated more electricity than coal in the US for the first time in May
summary: In May, solar supplied 12.8% of US electricity, surpassing coal's 12.2% and becoming the nation's third-largest power source. This milestone highlights solar's continued growth despite federal policy.
details: For the first time in May, solar power supplied more electricity to the US grid than coal, marking a significant shift in the nation's energy landscape. Solar accounted for 12.8% of US electricity, while coal's share dropped to 12.2%, its fourth-lowest monthly share ever.

This achievement elevates solar to the third-largest source of electricity in the US, trailing only natural gas and nuclear power. The decline in coal generation, which hit an all-time monthly low in April, allowed solar to take a leading position.

The continued growth of solar power, which has been the leading source of new power for five years, occurs even as federal policies have aimed to boost the struggling coal industry. Solar and battery storage made up 91% of all new generating capacity in Q1.

Experts anticipate more months where solar generation will exceed coal, with a projected annual overtake within a few years. This trend is significant as US electricity demand is rising due to AI, domestic manufacturing, and the electrification of transport and heating.

Globally, renewable energy sources are rapidly expanding, with projections from the International Energy Agency indicating they will constitute almost 45% of global electricity generation by 2030. This underscores a worldwide shift towards cleaner energy.
